scrunch.whyHard: It is a made-up word. It is in the Centipede's song.

prock.whyHard: It is a made-up word. It is the name of a monster that the men shout.

gnormous.example: And that gnormous and gnorrible Gnat

gnorrible.whyHard: The writer adds a silent 'g', as a joke.
gnorrible.example: And that gnormous and gnorrible Gnat

sentipede.example: But they cent quite the wrong Sentipede!

paragraphs.context: Their troubles were all over in a jiffy
paragraphs.mainIdea: James's parents die, and James is left alone. He is sent to live with his two aunts.
paragraphs.simple: This was a bad thing for two such kind parents. But in the end it was much worse for James than for them. Their troubles were over very fast. They were dead and gone in thirty-five seconds. Poor James, on the other hand, was still alive. All at once he was alone and afraid in a huge world that was not kind. The lovely house by the sea had to be sold at once. The little boy took only a small suitcase with a pair of pyjamas and a toothbrush in it. He was sent away to live with his two aunts.

paragraphs.context: They were selfish and lazy and cruel, and right from the beginning
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker are very bad people. They are unkind to James from the start. They give him no toys or books.
paragraphs.simple: The aunts were called Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker. The writer says he is sorry, but they were both really horrible people. They were selfish and lazy and cruel. From the very start they hit poor James for almost no reason. They never used his real name. They always called him 'you disgusting little beast' or 'you filthy nuisance' or 'you miserable creature'. They never gave him any toys to play with or any picture books to look at. His room was as bare as a prison cell.

paragraphs.context: in a queer ramshackle house on the top of a high hill
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three of them live in a strange old house on a high hill. From the garden James can see far away, even the house where he used to live.
paragraphs.simple: Aunt Sponge, Aunt Spiker and now James lived in a strange old house that was falling apart. It was on top of a high hill in the south of England. The hill was so high that from almost anywhere in the garden James could look down and see for miles and miles over a wonderful land of woods and fields. On a very clear day he could see a tiny grey dot far away. It was the house where he used to live with his dear mother and father. Past that, he could see the ocean itself. It was a long thin line of dark blue-black, like a line of ink, under the edge of the sky.

paragraphs.context: an ancient peach tree that never gave any peaches
paragraphs.mainIdea: The garden is big and empty, with no toys and no other children. James is sad and lonely.
paragraphs.simple: The garden covered the whole top of the hill. It was large and empty. The only tree in the whole place was a very old peach tree that never gave any peaches. There were also some dirty old laurel bushes at the far end. There was no swing, no seesaw and no sand pit. No other children were asked to come up the hill to play with poor James. There was not even a dog or a cat to keep him company. As time went on, he became sadder and sadder and more and more lonely. He spent hours every day at the bottom of the garden. He looked sadly at the lovely world of woods and fields and ocean below him. He was not allowed to go there. It was spread out like a magic carpet.

paragraphs.context: She was like a great white soggy overboiled cabbage
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer describes the two aunts. Aunt Sponge is very fat and short. Aunt Spiker is thin and tall.
paragraphs.simple: Aunt Sponge was very fat and very short. She had small eyes like a pig's, a mouth that went in, and a soft white face that looked as if it had been boiled. She was like a great white wet cabbage that had been boiled too long. Aunt Spiker, on the other hand, was thin, tall and bony. She wore glasses with steel rims that were held on the end of her nose with a clip. She had a loud sharp voice and long wet thin lips. When she got angry or excited, small bits of spit shot out of her mouth as she talked. There the two horrible old women sat, drinking their drinks. Every now and again they screamed at James to chop faster and faster. They also talked about themselves. Each one said how beautiful she thought she was.

paragraphs.context: Poor James was still slaving away at the chopping-block
paragraphs.mainIdea: James works hard in the heat. He feels sad and thinks about other children who are happy.
paragraphs.simple: Poor James was still working very hard at the chopping-block. The heat was terrible. He was wet all over with sweat. His arm hurt. The chopper was big and not sharp, and far too heavy for a small boy to use. As he worked, James began to think about all the other children in the world. He wondered what they might be doing now. Some would be riding tricycles in their gardens. Some would be walking in cool woods and picking bunches of wild flowers. All the little friends he used to know would be down by the sea, playing in the wet sand and splashing around in the water.

paragraphs.context: an old man in a funny dark-green suit emerging from the bushes
paragraphs.mainIdea: A strange old man comes out of the bushes and stares hard at James.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly, just behind him, James heard leaves moving. He turned round and saw an old man in a funny dark green suit coming out of the bushes. The old man was very small, but he had a huge head with no hair on top. His face was covered all over with stiff black hair. He stopped when he was about three yards away. He stood there, leaning on his stick and looking hard at James.

paragraphs.context: a mass of tiny green things that looked like little stones or crystals
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old man shows James a bag of tiny green things. They look like stones, and they shine in a wonderful way.
paragraphs.simple: 'Take a look, my dear,' he said. He opened the bag and tipped it toward James. Inside it, James could see many tiny green things. They looked like little stones or crystals. Each one was about the size of a grain of rice. They were very, very beautiful. They had a strange brightness, a kind of light that made them shine and sparkle in a wonderful way.

paragraphs.context: One thousand long slimy crocodile tongues boiled up in the skull
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old man says what the green things are made of. He names many strange things, such as crocodile tongues.
paragraphs.simple: 'You would never guess that!' the old man whispered. He bent down a little and pushed his face closer and closer to James. At last the tip of his long nose touched the skin on James's forehead. Then he jumped back and waved his stick madly in the air. 'Crocodile tongues!' he shouted. 'One thousand long slimy crocodile tongues, boiled for twenty days and nights in the skull of a dead witch, with the eyeballs of a lizard! Add the fingers of a young monkey, the gizzard of a pig, the beak of a green parrot, the juice of a porcupine, and three spoons of sugar. Stew for another week, and then let the moon do the rest!'

paragraphs.context: pour all the little green things into it. Then, very slowly, one by one
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old man tells James what to do with the green things. If the green things get away, their magic will go to someone else.
paragraphs.simple: 'And now,' the old man said, 'all you have to do is this. Take a large jug of water and pour all the little green things into it. Then, very slowly, one by one, add ten hairs from your own head. That starts them! In a few minutes the water will begin to bubble very hard. As soon as that happens, you must quickly drink it all down, the whole jug, in one big drink. Then you will feel it moving and boiling in your stomach, and steam will start coming out of your mouth. Right after that, wonderful, unbelievable things will start happening to you. You will never be sad again in your life. Because you are sad, aren't you? You do not need to tell me! I know all about it! Now go and do just what I say. And do not say a word of this to those two horrible aunts of yours! And do not let those green things get away from you! If they do get away, their magic will work on someone else instead of you. The first one they meet, a bug, an insect, an animal or a tree, will get the full power of their magic. So hold the bag tight! Do not tear the paper! Go! Hurry up! Do not wait! Now is the time! Hurry!'

paragraphs.context: They were all sinking into the soil! He could actually see them wriggling
paragraphs.mainIdea: The green things go into the ground. James tries to catch them, but they are too fast.
paragraphs.simple: James got up on to his hands and knees at once and began looking for his precious treasures. But what was this? They were all sinking into the soil! He could see them moving and turning as they dug their way down into the hard earth. At once he reached out a hand to pick some of them up before it was too late, but they went away right under his fingers. He went after some others, and the same thing happened! He tried hard to catch the ones that were left, but they were too quick for him. Each time the tips of his fingers were just about to touch them, they were gone into the earth! Soon, in only a few seconds, every single one of them had gone!

paragraphs.context: They were like a couple of hunters who had just shot an elephant
paragraphs.mainIdea: The aunts walk round the huge peach and look at it with great care. They are like hunters who have shot an elephant and do not know if it is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker began to walk slowly round the peach. They looked at it very carefully from every side. They were like two hunters who had just shot an elephant and were not quite sure if it was dead or alive. The huge round fruit was so tall above them that they looked like very small people from another world beside it.

paragraphs.context: these two crafty women stationed themselves at the front gate
paragraphs.mainIdea: The aunts build a fence round the peach and make people pay to come in.
paragraphs.simple: Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker quickly called in carpenters, men who work with wood. They had the men build a strong fence round the peach to keep it safe from the crowd. At the same time, these two clever, tricky women stood at the front gate with a large bunch of tickets. They started charging everyone money to come in.

paragraphs.context: Everything is so deadly quiet, and the shadows are so long and black
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many people, most of all small children, are afraid to be outside alone in the moonlight.
paragraphs.simple: Most people, and small children most of all, are often quite afraid of being outside alone in the moonlight. Everything is so very quiet. The shadows are so long and black, and they keep turning into strange shapes that seem to move as you look at them. The smallest snap of a stick makes you jump.

paragraphs.context: damp and murky, and all around him there was the curious bittersweet smell
paragraphs.mainIdea: James is in the tunnel in the peach. It is wet and dark, and the peach juice tastes very good.
paragraphs.simple: The tunnel was wet and dark. All round him there was the strange smell of fresh peach, sweet with a little bitter in it. The floor was soft and wet under his knees. The walls were wet and sticky, and peach juice was dripping from the ceiling. James opened his mouth and caught some of it on his tongue. It tasted very good.

paragraphs.context: was at least as big as James himself, and in the strange greenish light
paragraphs.mainIdea: The creatures are as big as James. In the strange green light they look very frightening.
paragraphs.simple: Every one of these 'creatures' was at least as big as James himself. A strange green light shone down from somewhere in the ceiling. In that light they looked very, very frightening to look at.

paragraphs.context: We wouldn’t dream of hurting you. You are one of us now
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Ladybird tells James not to be afraid. She says he is now one of them.
paragraphs.simple: 'You must not be afraid,' the Ladybird said kindly. 'We would never hurt you. You are one of us now. Didn't you know that? You are one of the crew. We are all in the same boat.'

paragraphs.context: He simply cannot stop telling lies about his legs
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Earthworm says the Centipede tells lies about his legs. He does not have a hundred. He has only forty-two.
paragraphs.simple: 'There he goes again!' the Earthworm cried. It was the first time he had spoken. 'He cannot stop telling lies about his legs! He does not have anything like a hundred of them! He has only forty-two! The trouble is that most people do not take the trouble to count them. They just believe what he says. And anyway, Centipede, there is nothing wonderful about having a lot of legs.'

paragraphs.context: the only thing that has been stopping this peach from rolling away
paragraphs.mainIdea: The garden is on a steep slope. Only the thick stem stops the peach from rolling away.
paragraphs.simple: 'You may not have seen it,' the Ladybird went on, 'but the whole garden, even before it gets to the steep edge of the hill, is on a steep slope. So the only thing that has stopped this peach from rolling away from the very beginning is the thick stem that holds it to the tree. Break the stem, and off we go.'

paragraphs.context: will always keep on rolling as long as it is on a downhill slope
paragraphs.mainIdea: A round thing keeps rolling down a slope. Here the land goes down all the way to the ocean that James had asked to visit.
paragraphs.simple: Why should it? A round thing will always keep on rolling as long as it is on a slope that goes down. Here the land went down all the way until it came to the ocean. It was the same ocean that James had asked his aunts so much to let him visit the day before.

paragraphs.context: Everything and all of them were being rattled around like peas inside
paragraphs.mainIdea: The trip down the hill is terrible. Everyone and everything is thrown around inside the peach.
paragraphs.simple: But when the peach left the garden and went rushing down the steep hill, the whole thing became a nightmare. James found himself thrown up against the ceiling, then back on to the floor, then sideways against the wall, then up to the ceiling again. He went up and down and back and forth and round and round. At the same time all the other creatures were flying through the air in every direction. So were the chairs and the sofa, and the forty-two boots of the Centipede. Everything and all of them were shaken like peas inside a huge rattle that a mad giant would not stop shaking. To make it worse, something went wrong with the Glow-worm's light, and the room was completely dark. There were screams and shouts and bad words and cries of pain. Everything kept going round and round. Once James made a wild grab at some thick bars sticking out from the wall, but they were two of the Centipede's legs. 'Let go, you idiot!' shouted the Centipede, kicking himself free. James was at once thrown across the room into the hard lap of the Old-Green-Grasshopper. Twice he got caught in Miss Spider's legs, which was a horrible thing. Near the end, the poor Earthworm cracked himself like a whip each time he flew from one side of the room to the other. In a panic he wrapped himself round James's body and would not let go.

paragraphs.context: A strong current and a high wind had carried the peach so quickly away
paragraphs.mainIdea: The peach is far from land. Only the ocean can be seen all round.
paragraphs.simple: And they were. A strong current and a high wind had carried the peach so quickly away from the land that it was already out of sight. All round them lay the huge black ocean, deep and hungry. Little waves were moving against the sides of the peach.

paragraphs.context: give someone enough balloons to hold, I mean really enough, then up he goes
paragraphs.mainIdea: James says there are plenty of seagulls. If there is time, enough seagulls can lift the peach, like balloons.
paragraphs.simple: 'There are plenty of seagulls,' James answered. 'Look for yourself. We will probably need four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, maybe even a thousand. I do not know. I will just keep joining them to the stem until we have enough to lift us. In the end they must lift us. It is like balloons. If you give someone enough balloons to hold, really enough, then up he goes. And a seagull can lift much more than a balloon. If only we have the time. If only those awful sharks do not sink us first.'

paragraphs.context: It was like a delicately balanced scale that needed only the tiniest push
paragraphs.mainIdea: The peach is just touching the water. A tiny push can send it up or down.
paragraphs.simple: The bottom of the peach was just touching the water. It was like a scale that was carefully balanced. It needed only the smallest push to tip it one way or the other.

paragraphs.context: A shark, you see, has an extremely long sharp nose, and its mouth
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says why the sharks could not hurt the peach. Their noses get in the way.
paragraphs.simple: This was closer to the truth than any of them knew. A shark has a very long sharp nose. Its mouth is under its face, a long way back. So it can hardly get its teeth into a huge smooth round thing like the side of a peach. Even if the shark turns on to its back, it still cannot do it, because its nose is always in the way. Think of a small dog that tries to get its teeth into a very big ball. That is about how it was with the sharks and the peach.

paragraphs.context: whatever might be lurking secretly up there in the great cloud-mountains
paragraphs.mainIdea: A plane is loud, so what hides in the clouds runs away. That is why people in planes never see anything.
paragraphs.simple: There was no sound anywhere. Travelling on the peach was not at all like travelling in a plane. A plane comes loud and noisy through the sky. Anything that may be hiding up there in the great cloud-mountains runs away when the plane comes near. That is why people who travel in planes never see anything.

paragraphs.context: wispy, wraithlike, shadowy, white creatures who looked as though they were made out of
paragraphs.mainIdea: James and his friends see tall, thin, white creatures on a cloud. They look like cotton wool, candyfloss and thin white hairs.
paragraphs.simple: Once, as they went quietly past a huge white cloud, they saw a group of strange, tall, thin things on the top of it. The things were about twice as tall as ordinary men. They were not easy to see at first, because they were almost as white as the cloud itself. But as the peach came closer, it was clear that these 'things' were living creatures. They were tall, thin, white and like shadows. They looked as though they were made of a mixture of cotton wool and candyfloss and thin white hairs.

paragraphs.context: the whole underneath of the cloud seemed to split and burst open like
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge mass of water falls from a cloud onto the peach. The seagulls fly through it, and the peach sails on.
paragraphs.simple: Three seconds later, the whole bottom of the cloud seemed to split and burst open like a paper bag, and out came the water! They saw it coming. It was not just raindrops. It was a great solid mass of water, like a lake or a whole ocean, falling out of the sky on top of them. It came down and down. It crashed first on to the seagulls and then on to the peach. The poor travellers screamed with fear and felt around wildly for something to hold: the peach stem, the silk strings, anything. All the time the water poured and roared down on them. It was like being held down under the biggest waterfall in the world and not being able to get out. They could not speak. They could not see. They could not breathe. Holding on madly to one of the silk strings, James told himself that this must be the end of everything. But then, as suddenly as it had started, the water stopped. They were out of it, and it was all over. The wonderful seagulls had flown right through it and come out safely on the other side. Once again the giant peach was sailing quietly through the mysterious sky in the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: They saw the huge drums that were used for making thunder
paragraphs.mainIdea: James and his friends see the world of the Cloud-Men. The Cloud-Men make snow, thunder, frost and storms. They also have a city, with caves, wives and children.
paragraphs.simple: Once they passed a snow machine at work. The Cloud-Men were turning the handle, and a storm of snowflakes was blowing out of the big funnel above. They saw the huge drums used for making thunder, and the Cloud-Men hitting them hard with long hammers. They saw the frost factories, and the places that make wind, and the places where cyclones and tornadoes were made and sent spinning down to the Earth. Once, deep in a large soft cloud, they saw what could only be a city of the Cloud-Men. There were caves everywhere going into the cloud. At the door of each cave, the Cloud-Men's wives were bending over little stoves with frying-pans in their hands. They were frying snowballs for their husbands' suppers. Hundreds of the Cloud-Men's children were playing all over the place, shouting with laughter and sliding down the soft hills of the cloud on toboggans.

sentences.context: Both of them suddenly got eaten up
sentences.simple: An enormous angry rhinoceros ate both of them all of a sudden. It happened in full daylight, on a street full of people. It had got out of the zoo in London.
sentences.grammar: 'got eaten up' means 'were eaten up': it tells what happened to the parents, and the rhinoceros did the eating.

sentences.context: far nastier for James than it was for them
sentences.simple: But in the end it was much worse for James than it was for them.
sentences.grammar: 'far' makes 'nastier' stronger, so it means 'much nastier'; 'than' is used to compare James with his parents.

sentences.context: carrying nothing but a small suitcase
sentences.simple: The little boy was sent away to live with his two aunts. He had only a small suitcase, with a pair of pyjamas and a toothbrush in it.
sentences.grammar: 'carrying nothing but a small suitcase' tells what the boy had with him; the main action is 'was sent away'.

sentences.context: Neither Aunt Sponge nor Aunt Spiker could ever be bothered
sentences.simple: Neither Aunt Sponge nor Aunt Spiker ever wanted to take the trouble to take him out, not even for a small walk or a picnic. And he was not allowed to go alone.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither ... nor' means not the first and not the second; 'could never be bothered' means 'never wanted to take the trouble'.

sentences.context: if he even so much as dared to climb over the fence
sentences.simple: The aunts said terrible punishments would come if he even tried to climb over the fence. One was to be locked in the cellar with the rats for a week.
sentences.grammar: 'even so much as' means 'even just', so a very small act is enough to bring the punishment; 'dared to' means 'was brave enough to'.

sentences.context: soon caused a second thing to happen which was very peculiar
sentences.simple: This first thing was only a little strange. But it soon made a second thing happen, and that second thing was very strange.
sentences.grammar: 'caused a second thing to happen' means 'made a second thing happen'; 'which was very peculiar' tells about the second thing, not the first.

sentences.context: whenever she got angry or excited
sentences.simple: Each time she got angry or excited, small bits of spit shot out of her mouth when she talked.
sentences.grammar: 'whenever' means 'each time'; 'would come shooting' uses 'would' for something that happened again and again in the past.

sentences.context: Such loveliness as I possess can only truly shine
sentences.simple: A beauty like mine can only really shine in Hollywood.
sentences.grammar: 'Such loveliness as I have' means 'beauty like mine'; it is a very proud, old-style way to speak, as in a poem.

sentences.context: It was at this point that the first thing of all
sentences.simple: At this moment the first thing happened to him. It was the strange thing that led to many more, much stranger things.
sentences.grammar: 'It was ... that ...' puts the focus on 'at this point'; the part between the commas tells more about 'the first thing'.

sentences.context: than in all the rest of the world put together
sentences.simple: There is more power and magic in those things than in all the rest of the world added together.
sentences.grammar: 'more ... than' compares two amounts; 'put together' means 'added together'.

sentences.context: Whoever they meet first, be it bug, insect, animal, or tree
sentences.simple: The first one they meet will get the full power of their magic. It can be a bug, an insect, an animal or a tree.
sentences.grammar: 'Whoever' means 'any one that'; 'be it' is an old way to say 'whether it is'.

sentences.context: if they do escape, then they will be working their magic
sentences.simple: If they really get away, their magic will work on someone else instead of on you.
sentences.grammar: 'do escape' uses 'do' to make the verb stronger (if they really escape); 'will be working' means the work will be going on.

sentences.context: if only he could get in there without Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker seeing him
sentences.simple: He told himself he would do it all in the kitchen, but only if he could get in without Aunt Sponge and Aunt Spiker seeing him.
sentences.grammar: 'if only' shows a strong wish; 'without ... seeing him' means they do not see him.

sentences.context: if only he hadn’t slipped and fallen and dropped that precious bag
sentences.simple: He wished that he had not slipped and fallen and dropped the precious bag.
sentences.grammar: 'if only + had + done' is a wish about the past. It cannot change now.

sentences.context: never even had a blossom on it, let alone a peach
sentences.simple: That tree has never even had a flower on it, and certainly not a peach.
sentences.grammar: 'let alone' means 'and certainly not'; 'tree’s never had' means 'tree has never had'.

sentences.context: He hadn’t the faintest idea what it might be
sentences.simple: He had no idea what it might be, but he felt in his bones that something would happen soon.
sentences.grammar: 'hadn’t the faintest idea' is an old-style British way to say 'had no idea at all'; 'might' shows he is not sure.

sentences.context: as clearly as if it were a balloon being blown up
sentences.simple: He could see the peach getting bigger and bigger, as clearly as if it were a balloon that someone was filling with air.
sentences.grammar: 'as if it were' compares with something not real, and 'were' is used for this; 'being blown up' means someone is putting air in it.

sentences.context: as large and round and fat as Aunt Sponge herself
sentences.simple: A minute later, this huge fruit was as big and round and fat as Aunt Sponge, and probably as heavy.
sentences.grammar: 'as + big + as' says two things are the same; 'herself' puts the focus on Aunt Sponge.

sentences.context: something extremely hard blocking his way
sentences.simple: The top of his head hit something very hard that was in his way.
sentences.grammar: 'blocking his way' is an extra part that tells more about 'something extremely hard'.

sentences.context: thinking he could bolt back into the tunnel the way he had come
sentences.simple: He looked behind him. He thought he could run back into the tunnel the way he came, but the door was gone.
sentences.grammar: 'bolt' here means 'run away fast'; 'the way he had come' means 'by the same path he used before'.

sentences.context: So what would you call it if you saw a grasshopper
sentences.simple: So what would you call a grasshopper as large as a dog, if you saw one?
sentences.grammar: 'would ... if ... saw' is for something not real: 'if' + past, 'would' + verb.

sentences.context: I do believe he thinks it’s him that we are wanting to eat
sentences.simple: I really think he thinks that we want to eat him!
sentences.grammar: 'do believe' is stronger than 'believe'; 'it’s him that ...' puts the focus on 'him'.

sentences.context: for the life of me I cannot understand why
sentences.simple: I cannot understand why, however hard I try.
sentences.grammar: 'for the life of me' is an idiom that makes 'cannot' stronger: I cannot, however hard I try.

sentences.context: But he is long past it now
sentences.simple: But he is much too old to be a pest now.
sentences.grammar: 'past it' means 'too old to do it', and 'it' is being a pest; 'long' means for a long time.

sentences.context: suspended by a rope of threads at either end
sentences.simple: It hung from the ceiling, held up by a rope of threads at each end. So it looked more like a hammock than a bed.
sentences.grammar: 'suspended' means hung from above; 'either end' means each of the two ends.

sentences.context: to make matters worse, all the laces were tied up
sentences.simple: Each boot had laces that had to be untied and loosened before it came off. To make it worse, all the laces were tied in very hard knots that had to be picked open with fingernails.
sentences.grammar: 'to make matters worse' means 'and what was worse'; 'had to be unpicked' means someone had to pick the knots open.

sentences.context: is up there on top of the peach nibbling away at that stem
sentences.simple: At this moment our Centipede, who has jaws as sharp as razors, is on top of the peach. He is biting away at the stem little by little.
sentences.grammar: 'who has ... razors' between commas adds news about the Centipede; 'is ... nibbling away' shows it is happening now.

sentences.context: Just wait till I get my hands on him
sentences.simple: Just wait until I catch him.
sentences.grammar: 'wait till' is followed by 'get', not 'will get'; 'get my hands on him' means 'catch him' and sounds like a threat.

sentences.context: no travellers had ever had a more terrible journey than
sentences.simple: In the whole history of the world, no travellers had a worse journey than these poor creatures.
sentences.grammar: 'no ... ever had a more ... than' is a way to say it was the worst; 'had had' is the past perfect, about a time before the story moment.

sentences.context: It’s taken years off my life
sentences.simple: The trip was very bad for her. She says it took years off her life.
sentences.grammar: 'It’s taken' means 'It has taken'; 'take years off my life' is a joke way to say the trip hurt her a lot.

sentences.context: I am slowly shrivelling up for want of food
sentences.simple: I am slowly getting dry and small because I have no food.
sentences.grammar: 'for want of' means 'because there is not enough of'; 'am shrivelling' shows it is happening now.

sentences.context: to make any sort of a dent in this enormous peach
sentences.simple: It would take us weeks and weeks to make even a small hole in this huge peach.
sentences.grammar: 'It would take us weeks to ...' says how long it takes; 'make a dent in' means 'make a small mark in'.

sentences.context: How on earth do you propose to get a loop of string
sentences.simple: How do you plan to put a loop of string round a seagull’s neck? I suppose you will fly up there yourself and catch it!
sentences.grammar: 'How on earth' shows strong surprise; 'propose to + verb' means 'plan to + verb'.

sentences.context: what difference does it make whether it’s sharks or seagulls
sentences.simple: You will be eaten anyway. So it does not matter if it is sharks or seagulls.
sentences.grammar: 'what difference does it make' means 'it does not matter'; 'whether ... or ...' gives two choices.

sentences.context: because the nose always gets in the way
sentences.simple: Even if the shark turns on to its back, it still cannot do it, because its nose is always in the way.
sentences.grammar: 'Even if ... still' means the change does not help; 'gets in the way' means 'is in the way'.

sentences.context: A large hailstone can hurt you as much as a rock
sentences.simple: A large hailstone can hurt you as much as a rock or a lump of lead, if someone throws it hard enough.
sentences.grammar: 'as much as' says two things are the same; 'if it is thrown hard enough' means 'if someone throws it hard enough'.

sentences.context: got tangled up with the silk strings
sentences.simple: The ropes that the Cloud-Men had used to lower the rainbow got caught in a knot with the silk strings that went up from the peach to the seagulls.
sentences.grammar: 'got tangled up' means 'became tangled up'; 'had been using' shows they were using the ropes before this moment.

sentences.context: he must weigh almost nothing at all for one seagull to be able to pull him up
sentences.simple: He must weigh almost nothing at all, because one seagull can pull him up like that.
sentences.grammar: 'must' here means 'I am sure'; 'for one seagull to be able to pull him up' gives the reason for what James thinks.

go on.meaning: To keep going. It can also mean to tell someone to say or do more.

give up.meaning: To stop trying. Here, it means you cannot find the answer.

look out.meaning: Words you say to tell someone to be careful.

hold on.meaning: To hold something hard so you do not fall.

take off.meaning: To take clothes off your body.

pull off.meaning: To take something off by pulling it.
pull off.example: before it could be pulled off

put out.meaning: To make a light stop shining.

come along.example: have come along to say hello

turn round.meaning: To move your body to face the other way.
turn round.example: he turned round and saw an old man

wake up.meaning: To stop sleeping, or to make someone stop sleeping.

sit down.meaning: To move your body down into a seat or onto the floor.

cheer up.meaning: To feel happier, or to make someone feel happier.

pick up.meaning: To take something up with your hand.

climb over.meaning: To go up and across something, such as a wall.
climb over.example: dared to climb over the fence

run out of.meaning: To have no more of something.

break out.meaning: To start suddenly. It is used for bad things, such as a fight or fear.

gobble up.example: gobble up all the nasty little insects

eat up.example: come along to eat us up

get over.meaning: To feel well again after something bad.

get away.meaning: To get free and go away.

get in the way.meaning: To be in someone's way and stop them from doing something.

make a fortune.meaning: To get a lot of money.
make a fortune.example: We shall make a fortune today

in a jiffy.meaning: Very soon. In a very short time.
in a jiffy.example: I’ll be back in a jiffy

on the other hand.meaning: Used to show a different thing or a different side.
on the other hand.example: Aunt Spiker, on the other hand, was lean

for the life of me.example: for the life of me I cannot understand why

in the same boat.example: We’re all in the same boat.

be bound to.meaning: To be sure to do something.
